Mesophilic aerobic digestion: An efﬁcient and inexpensive biological
pretreatment to improve biogas production from highly-recalcitrant
pinewood
Kavosh Karami a, Keikhosro Karimi a, b, Safoora Mirmohamadsadeghi a, Rajeev Kumar c, *
a Department of Chemical Engineering, Isfahan University of Technology, Isfahan, 84156-83111, Iran
b Department of Chemical Engineering, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, 1050, Brussels, Belgium
c Center for Environmental Research and Technology (CE-CERT), Bourns College of Engineering, University of California Riverside, Riverside, CA, 92507, USA
a r t i c l e
i n f o

Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Biogas
Alkaline pretreatment
Aerobic digestion
Ultrasonication
a b s t r a c t
Biological pretreatments and their combination with chemical and physical pretreatments are among the
inexpensive methods for the improvement of biogas production from lignocellulosic biomass. In this
study, mesophilic aerobic digestion was studied as a biological pretreatment to improve biogas pro-
duction from pinewood. Its effects in combination with other pretreatments, i.e., liquid hot water (LHW),
sodium hydroxide (NaOH), and ultrasonic pretreatments, were also investigated. LHW and Alkali (using
8% w/w NaOH) pretreatments were performed at less severe conditions (100 C for 10 min) to evaluate
the synergistic effect of these thermochemical pretreatments on biogas production. The ultrasonic
pretreatment was performed at 40 KHz for 30 min at 40 C. Biological pretreatment was carried out using
aerobic sludge at 37 C for 10 days. The aerobic digestion was the only pretreatment that could indi-
vidually improve the methane yield from pinewood by 7.3 folds. However, the highest methane yield
(57.7 mL/g VS of pretreated pinewood) was obtained by the combination of NaOH, biological, and ul-
trasonic pretreatments, which was 11.2 folds higher than that of the untreated substrate. It was
concluded that the pretreatment with aerobic digestion could signiﬁcantly improve the biogas pro-
duction yield, especially in combination with mild thermo-chemical pretreatments.

1. Introduction
Increase in human activities and the use of unsustainable fossil
fuels have caused changes in the climate of the planet [1,2]. This
drew attention towards clean and renewable biofuels such as
ethanol and biogas that are not only sustainable but can mitigate
the
climate
issues
also
[3,4].
Biogas,
as
one
of
the
most
environmentally-friendly biofuels, is mainly composed of methane
and is produced from the anaerobic digestion of organic materials
[5,6].
One of the best sources of organic materials for biogas produc-
tion is lignocellulosic materials. Lignocellulosic biomass, including
forestry, agricultural, and industrial wastes, is an abundant and
inexpensive renewable source of organic materials. Nonetheless, in
addition to clean and inexpensive fuel production, utilization of
these wastes for biofuels production greatly reduces the environ-
mental problems caused due to the accumulation of these wastes
[7].
One of the advantages of woody biomass among other ligno-
celluloses, e.g, agricultural residue such corn stover and wheat
straw, is its non-seasonal nature. Woods are divided into two cat-
egories: softwoods and hardwoods. Generally, lignin content in
softwoods is higher than that of hardwoods. Besides, liginin in
softwoods is more complex and difﬁcult to separate. This leads to
the requirement of more severe pretreatments on softwoods to
increase their digestibility [8].
Although softwood is too difﬁcult to biodegrade due to its highly
recalcitrant structure [9], pinewood waste, softwood, is a ligno-
cellulosic compound that can be used as a substrate for biogas
production. The main constituents of lignocellulosic materials are
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [10]. The strong crystalline
structure of cellulose surrounded by lignin and hemicellulose
makes a recalcitrant structure that is difﬁcult to be converted to

biogas by anaerobic bacteria [11]. Therefore, to overcome this
problem, it is necessary to pretreat the pinewood prior to biogas
production to increase its digestibility [12]. The purpose of pre-
treatments is to improve the substrate bio-digestibility by dis-
rupting the biomass complex structure as well as by changing the
cellulose crystallinity and structure [13,14].
Different types of pretreatments including physical, chemical,
physicochemical, biological, and combination of these have been
developed over the years [15]. Physical pretreatments, such as
grinding and irradiation, usually improve the biomass digestibility
through physical breakdown, resizing, crystallinity reduction,
increasing the available surface area, and enhancing the biomass
pore size [16]. Among physical pretreatments, ultrasonic pretreat-
ment has been commonly used to improve mass transfer in
chemical pretreatments. It also forms cavitation bubbles which
mechanically disrupt the lignocellulose cell wall [17]. This process
can be used to improve biogas production from residual crops,
grass, and activated sludge [18]. Ultrasound can be combined with
other pretreatments, which provides some advantages, such as the
reduction of pretreatment time, temperature, and the amount of
chemicals [19]. On the other hand, alkaline pretreatment using
sodium hydroxide is one of the widely used thermochemical pre-
treatments for lignocelluloses. This pretreatment can reduce the
lignin content in addition to reduction in cellulose crystallinity. It
also increases the biomass porosity and reduces particle size, which
result in enhanced digestibility of biomass [20]. Liquid hot water
pretreatment is a widely applied physico-chemical pretreatment in
which high pressure is applied to maintain water in liquid phase at
elevated temperatures [21]. In this process, the mixture of biomass
and water is cooked at high temperature and pressure. This type of
pretreatment has the potential to increase cellulose degradation
and biomass sugar extraction [22,23].
Although most thermochemical pretreatments are very effec-
tive in enhancing lignocellulosic biomass biological conversion,
they are typically very energy and capital intensive [24]. Biological
pretreatments, on the other hand, are less energy intensive and are
more
environmentally
friendly
than
thermochemical
pre-
treatments [25]. Different bacteria in aerobic sludge (including
Pseudomonadaceae, Azotobacter, and Neisseriaceae) were involved
in the degradation of lignin and wood structure [26]. Sharma et al.
[27] have comprehensively reviewed the biological pretreatments
of lignocelluloses. According to this review paper, depending upon
the type of microbes used for pretreatment, i.e., monoculture, co-
culture, and genetically engineered microbes, biological pre-
treatments can be categorized into various types. In co-culture
pretreatment, ﬁnding appropriate microorganisms for co-culture
is a challenge [27]. However, aerobic sludge is a microbial con-
sortium that has the ability to live symbiotically, and can be used
for biological pretreatment. Thus, in this research, aerobic digestion
using the aerobic sludge is proposed as a biological pretreatment to
improve the hydrolysis and the digestibility of pinewood.
According to the author's best knowledge, aerobic digestion has
not been previously investigated as a biological pretreatment to
improve biogas production. The present study aimed at investi-
gating the effect of aerobic digestion of pinewood on biogas pro-
duction. Due to the highly recalcitrant structure of the softwood
pinewood and the low speed of biological pretreatments, the aer-
obic digestion was also studied in combination with other widely
applied pretreatment methods. Ultrasound, sodium hydroxide, and
liquid hot water pretreatments were chosen as the widely applied
physical, chemical, and physicochemical pretreatments, respec-
tively, to be used prior to the biological pretreatment to ﬁnd the
optimum combined pretreatment method for biogas production
from pinewood. The structural changes of pinewood caused by the
pretreatments were investigated using compositional analysis,
scanning
electron
microscope
(SEM),
and
Fourier-transform
infrared spectroscopy (FTIR).
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and sludge
The feedstock was prepared from a 10-year-old pinewood tree
harvested from the Forest of Isfahan University of Technology. It
was dried at 45 C for 24 h, debarked, and cut into small pieces
using a carpentry chopper (Rasha WSH-T64, Iran). The chopped
pieces were powdered using a grinder (Bosch MKM6003, Ger-
many), screened using the Mesh 20 sieve, and stored in air-tight
plastic bags for further uses. The moisture (or solid) content of
the samples was measured by drying them at 105 C for 6 h.
Aerobic sludge and anaerobic sludge, obtained from the indus-
trial scale bioreactors of the North of Isfahan Wastewater Treat-
ment Plant, working at mesophilic conditions, were used for the
biological pretreatment and biogas production, respectively. Aero-
bic sludge was ﬁltered twice with 20 mesh screen and applied as
the inoculum for aerobic digestion. Anaerobic sludge and rumen
content were mixed at a weight ratio of 10:1, ﬁltered two times
with 20 mesh screen, and stored in dark bottle for 5 d prior to
applying as inoculum for anaerobic digestion.
2.2. Pretreatments
The order of the applied pretreatment methods was LHW/
NaOH-pretreatment,
biological
pretreatment,
and
ultrasonic
pretreatment.
2.2.1. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) pretreatment
For alkali pretreatment, pinewood (5 g) was presoaked in 8% wt.
sodium hydroxide solution (95 g) at room temperature for 10 min
with stirring. The pretreatment conditions were choosen based on
the optimum conditions reported by Salehian et al. [28]. The
mixture was then poured in a stainless steel reactor (500 mL, Steel
Sanat, Isfahan, Iran) and heated up to 100 C using an oil bath
(Memmert O200, Germany) and hold at this temperature for
10 min. After completion of the pretreatment, the reactor was
cooled down in an ice bath, and the mixture was centrifuged at
4500 rpm for 15 min (SELECTALAB, TDZ5-WS, China) at room
temperature to separate the solids from liquid phase. The liquid
portion was discarded and the pretreated solids were washed
repeatedly with room temperature distilled water until the pH of
supernatant was close to neutral. Finally, the washed pretreated
solids were frozen in liquid nitrogen, freeze-dried (Christ ALPHA
1e2 LD plus, Germany) for 48 h, and stored in plastic bags at 4 C for
further use.
2.2.2. Liquid hot water (LHW) pretreatment
For liquid hot water (LHW) pretreatment, all the steps of alka-
line pretreatment (section 2.2.1) were followed using distilled
water instead of alkaline solution. The pretreatment conditions
were based on the work by Safari et al. [29].
2.2.3. Biological pretreatment
Biological pretreatment was performed at 37 C and 90 rpm in a
shaker incubator (JAL TAJHIZ, Iran). For this, 20 mL aerobic sludge,
5 mL tap water, and untreated or pretreated pinewood (0.25 g dry
wt.) were added to the 118 mL open-cap bottles that were trans-
ferred to the shaker. The aerobic digestion pretreatment was run for
10 days in order to reach the equilibrium point of total volatile fatty
acids (VFAs) production. The VFAs production equilibrium point
was determined by performing elementary experiments. These

elementary experiments included kinetic studies during 25 days to
ﬁnd the day (10th day) that resulted in the maximum VFA con-
centration. The whole suspension obtained from biological pre-
treatment
was
used
for
further
stages
including
ultrasonic
pretreatment or anaerobic digestion.
2.2.4. Ultrasonic pretreatment
The untreated and pretreated substrates/slurry (0.25 g dry basis)
were added to tap water (5 mL) and were incubated in an ultrasonic
bath (Soltec SONICA 3200 L ETH S3, Italy,180 W) at the frequency of
40 KHz for 30 min at 40 C.
2.3. Biogas production
Untreated and pretreated pinewood solids were subjected to
anaerobic digestion for biogas production using batch fermenters
(118 mL dark-colored glass bottles) at mesophilic conditions ac-
cording to the Hansen et al.‘s approach [30]. All the anaerobic
digestion experiments were carried out in triplicates and the
average values are reported. The bottles, used as batch anaerobic
fermenters, were sealed by plastic caps and aluminum covers
during the anaerobic digestion experiments. In each bottle, 20 mL
of anaerobic sludge was added to 0.25 g substrate. Subsequently,
deionized water was added to the fermenters to bring the ﬁnal
volume to 25 mL. For biologically pretreated samples, 20 mL of
anaerobic sludge was added to the whole slurry obtained from
aerobic digestion. A reference fermenter containing anaerobic
sludge, water, and pure cellulose was also run in parallel. Two blank
fermentations were also run each in duplicate to evaluate the
biogas production from aerobic and anaerobic sludge individually.
Anaerobic conditions were created by purging the fermenters
with 95% pure nitrogen for 2 min. The bottles were placed in an
incubator (JAL TAJHIZ, Iran) at 37 C and manually shaken every
day. The sampling for gas production was conducted every 3 days
for the ﬁrst the 15 days, and then every 5 days for 40 days
fermentation. Methane production yield was calculated and re-
ported in mL methane at normal conditions (0 C, 105 pa) per g VS
of untreated or pretreated substrate.
2.4. Calculation of gasoline equivalent
To determine the optimal pretreatment combination, the pro-
duced energy was calculated as gasoline equivalent from each
metric ton of pinewood for each process. For this calculation, lower
heating values of the fuels at 25 C and 1 bar, 32.7 MJ/m3 for
methane and 32.0 MJ/L for gasoline, were considered [31].

and lignin contents in untreated and treated pinewood were
determined based on the National Renewable Energy Laboratory
(NREL, Denver, Colorado) standard methods [32,33].
High-performance liquid chromatography, equipped with UV/
Vis and RI detectors (1260 Inﬁnity, Agilent, California, USA) and
Aminex HPX-87 P ion-exchange column (Bio-Rad, Richmond, Cal-
ifornia, USA), was used to determine the amounts of sugars in the
liquid samples. The column temperature was set at 85 C, and the
deionized water was used as an eluent at a ﬂow rate of 0.6 mL/min.
The composition of biogas produced in anaerobic digestion was
analyzed by a gas chromatograph (Teif Gostar Faraz Co. GC-2550TG,
Iran) equipped with a packed column (Porapak Q, 3 m length and
3 mm internal diameter, Taufkirchen, Germany) and a thermal
conductivity detector. The carrier gas helium was used at a ﬂow rate
of 20 mL/min. The temperature of the column, injector, and de-
tector was 50 C, 90 C, and 140 C, respectively. The gas samples
were injected into the device by a pressure-tight syringe (SGE
250 R-V-GT, Australia). This syringe provides sampling at the
reactor pressure. The analytical grade of methane was used as the
standard. All the results of the produced methane were reported at
the normal conditions (0 C, 105 pa).
The amount of total volatile fatty acids (TVFA) produced after
biological pretreatment was calculated according to the Lossie and
Pütz's method [27,34] by titrating the substrate with 0.1 N H2SO4. In
brief, 20 mL of the fermented slurry was measured and placed on a
magnetic stirrer to homogenize during titration. In the ﬁrst step,
the titration continued until the pH reached 5, and the amount of
acid consumed was noted. After that, the titration continued until
the pH reached 4.4, and again the acid consumed was noted. Finally,
based on the volume of acid consumed, TVFA was calculated [34].
Also, the amount of each fatty acid produced during the biological
pretreatment was determined daily by withdrawing a 2 mL sample,
centrifuging, and injecting the supernatant into a gas chromato-
graph equipped with FID (Beifen Ruili Analytical 197 Instrument
Co., Beijing, China) and SolGel-WAX column (30 m length, 0.25 mm
internal diameter, 0.25 mm ﬁlm, SGE, Victoria, Australia).
The structural changes in pinewood caused by pretreatments
were investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, XL 30,
Eindhoven, Netherlands). The freeze-dried samples were mounted
on double-sided tape and placed on an aluminum base. The sam-
ples were coated with gold and analyzed by scanning electron
microscopy at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. The crystallinity and
structural changes of pinewood after NaOH and LHW treatments
were also examined using a Fourier transform infrared (FTIR, WQF-
510 A, Rayleigh Analytical Instrument Co., China) spectrometer
equipped with a universal ATR (UV-1601, Beifen Ruili Analytical 197
Instrument Co., Beijing, China) accessory and DGTS detector. The
FTIR spectra were obtained with an average of 64 scans in the range
of 600e4000 cm1 and a resolution of 2 cm1.
2.6. Statistical analysis
All experiments were carried out in triplicate and the average
values were reported. Minitab 19.2.0 software (Minitab Inc., State
College, USA) was used for the statistical analysis of the laboratory
data using analysis of variance (ANOVA) test and general linear
model (GLM). The Tukey method (with p < 0.05) was applied to
estimate and compare the signiﬁcant differences among the mean
values at 95% conﬁdence level. There are no signiﬁcant differences
(with p < 0.05) between the mean values with similar letter groups.
3. Results
3.1. Effect of pretreatments on pinewood composition and
structural characteristics
The structural changes of pinewood by LHW and NaOH pre-
treatments were investigated by compositional, FTIR, and SEM
analyses. The amounts of carbohydrates and lignin in untreated and
pretreated solids are presented in Table 1. The untreated pinewood
was determined to contain 31.7% total lignin and 62.1% carbohy-
drate, with glucan (40.5%) being the primary carbohydrate. Alkaline
pretreatment at 100 C for 10 min with 8% w/w NaOH mainly
decreased the lignin content from 31.7% to 24.2%. However, LHW
pretreatment mainly reduced xylan, galactan, and mannan con-
tents by 34.2% (from 7.3% to 4.8%), 65.6% (from 6.4% to 2.2%), and
67.1% (from 7.9% to 2.6%), respectively. As a result of lignin and
hemicellulose removal by NaOH and LHW pretreatments, respec-
tively, the corresponding glucan contents were increased up to 48.9
and 42.0% in the solids prepared by these pretreatments.
The effect of NaOH and LHW pretreatments on pinewood
structure was also investigated by FTIR analysis (Fig. 1 and Table 2).
This analysis is mainly used to determine the changes in the crys-
talline structure and surface functional groups caused by different
pretreatments on lignocelluloses. The peak at 898 cm1, which is
corresponding to the cellulose structure, decreased after pretreat-
ment. This conﬁms partial removal of cellulose due to the pre-
treatment with LHW and NaOH. Complete removal of the peak at
1725 cm1 was observed after NaOH pretreatment, suggesting the
removal of hemicellulose and lignin linkages. The crystallinity in-
dex is deﬁned as the ratio of the absorbance at 1098 cm1 to the
absorbance at 898 cm1, which represents cellulose type I and
cellulose type II, respectively. The crystallinity index of untreated
sample was 2.33, which decreased to 1.93 and 2.11 after NaOH and

LHW pretreatments, respectively. The total crystallinity index was
also calculated from the ratio of absorbance at the wavelength of

index values for untreated, NaOH-pretreated, and LHW-pretreated

SEM imaging of the samples was also carried out to investigate
the effect of pretreatments on the pinewood structure (Fig. 2). As
shown in Fig. 2, LHW pretreatment had a less destructive effect
than NaOH pretreatment. NaOH pretreatment degraded the sub-
strate structure and increased its digestibility by removing the
major porition of lignin and hemicellulose.
3.2. The effect of biological pretreatment on total volatile fatty acids
The amount of TVFAs produced from aerobic digestion (bio-
logical pretreatment) was evaluated and compared with that of
anaerobic digestion. The amount of TVFAs produced from the aer-
obic digestion of untreated wood was 50 mg acetic acid equivalent
(HAceq/L), and it was increased to 91 and 133 mg HAceq/L applying
LHW and NaOH pretreatments, respectively. These values were
considerably higher than those of anaerobic digestion (4, 11, and
25 mg HAceq/L, respectively). The VFAs are intermediate products of
anaerobic digestion, which are produced from the acidogenesis
stage. The higher content of TVFA produced from aerobic digestion
is an evidence of the ﬁrst two stages of digestion, i.e., hydrolysis and
acidogenesis.
The amounts of acetic acid and butyric acid, as the main con-
stitutes of TVFAs, produced during the aerobic digestion of pine-
wood are presented in Table 3. As the VFA production stopped and
the levels of butyric acid and acetic acid took a slight downward
trend (at the end of acidiﬁcation phase) after 10 days, aerobic
digestion was stopped. The values of acetic and butyric acids pro-
duced from NaOH and LHW pretreated pinewoods were consider-
ably higher than those of untreated samples. The acetic acid
concentrations were increased by 82.5% and 166.7% and butyric
acid concentrations were enhanced by 83.3% and 250.0% using
LHW and NaOH pretreatments, respectively.
3.3. Biogas production
The yields of methane produced during anaerobic digestion of
untreated and pretreated pinewood samples were determined and
are illustrated in Fig. 3. The highest methane yield of 57.7 mL/g VS of
pretreated pinewood was obtained using the combined pre-
treatments, including sodium hydroxide, aerobic digestion, and
ultrasonic pretreatments. The effectiveness of the biological pre-
treatment (aerobic digestion) in increasing the methane yield (by
7.3 folds) was considerably more than those of sodium hydroxide
and liquid hot water pretreatments, and even more than that of
ultrasonic pretreatment. At the ﬁrst look, it seems that all the
applied pretreatments, including biological, physical, chemical, and
physicochemical pretreatments, improved the methane production
yield. However, statistical analysis revealed that the individual ef-
fect of NaOH, LHW, and ultrasonic pretreatments was not signiﬁ-
cant (P < 0.05) on the improvement of methane yield. The methane
contents in the produced biogas (Table 4) were in the range of
59.1e70.3%. The combination of biological pretreatment with other
pretreatments considerably improved the biogas quality in all
cases.
3.4. Gasoline equivalent
The results for the equivalent gasoline volume are reported in
Table 4. Each metric ton of untreated pinewood produced 1.2 gal-
lons of gasoline. By LHW þ BP, 9.8 gallons of gasoline was produced.

Safari et al. [31] report 4.99 gallons of gasoline from pinewood in
the optimum pretreatment conditions (1% NaOH, 180 C, 5 h).
Whereas, the present study obtained 2.0 and 2.2 times higher
gasoline equivalents using LHW þ BP and NaOH þ BP pre-
treatments, respectively.
4. Discussion
The amount of pinewood wastes has increased within the past
decades due to its vast use in various industries. The highly recal-
citrant structure of pinewood, as a softwood, against microbial
conversion
promoted
this
research
to
ﬁnd
more
effective
pretreatments.
The NaOH and LHW pretreatments reduced the crystallinity
index of cellulose in pinewood by 17.2% and 9.4%, which is an evi-
dence of the partial conversion of type I cellulose to type II cellulose
in pinewood. In contrast, the corresponding total crystallinity in-
dexes of pinewood were increased by 11.4% and 10.5%. This can
mainly be due to the partial dissolution of lignin and hemicellulose
in the NaOH solution and LHW, respectively. Lignin and hemicel-
lulose are amorphous polymers that their removal causes higher
crystallinity in the residual lignocellulose solids and, therefore, a
higher total crystallinity index. NaOH pretreatment causes the
cleavage of ether and ester bindings in the lignin-carbohydrate
complexes and also CeC and ester linkages in lignin molecules
[35]. These chemical reactions lead to partial lignin removal that
was also shown with compositional analysis, which showed 23.3%
decrease in lignin content by alkaline pretreatment. LHW pre-
treatment cleaves the hemiacetal bindings in the lignocellulose
structure and causes acids formation [36]. The released acids break
the glycoside bindings in the hemicellulose structure, which causes
partial hemicellulose dissolution in the solution and decreases the
degree of polymerization of hemicellulose [37]. Hemicellulose
dissolution by LHW pretreatment was clearly revealed in the
composition of pinewood, in terms of decreasing the xylan, gal-
actan and mannan contents by 34.2, 65.6, and 67.1%, respectively.

The SEM images indicated that the alkaline pretreatment caused
more severe decomposition in pinewood structure compared to the
LHW pretreatment (Fig. 2). This was also conﬁrmed by the FTIR
(Table 2). The strong binding of Naþ and OH with water molecules
facilitates breaking down the hydrogen bonds within the wood

successful options. This was expected since mild conditions (100 C,
10 min) were chosen for those pretreatments that are not indi-
vidually appropriate options for the high recalcitrance structure of
pinewood. On the other hand, severe pretreatment conditions are
challenging for anaerobic digestion and can decrease methane yield
[38,39] due to inhibitors formation, total removal of hemicellulose,
and too high availability of organic materials that lead to over-
loading. Therefore, the combination of several mild pretreatments
can overcome these challenges.
The combination of NaOH, aerobic digestion, and ultrasonic
pretreatments resulted in the highest methane yield, which was
11.1 folds higher than that of untreated one. The NaOH pretreat-
ment removes lignin, increases porosity, and changes the chemical
structure of pinewood [40]. These modiﬁcations increase the
biomass porosity and access to carbohydrates for aerobic bacteria,
which hydrolyze the carbohydrates to smaller molecules. After
that, sonication makes further structural changes in the lignocel-
luloses and also causes the disintegration of aerobic sludge by
making bubbles and cavitation. The highest methane yields were
obtained from biological and ultrasonic pretreatment of LHW-
pretreated pinewood < biological and ultrasonic pretreatment of
pinewood < biological pretreatment of NaOH-pretreated pine-
wood. These three combined treatments increased methane pro-
duction yields by 8.99, 8.60, 9.52 folds, with no signiﬁcant
differences. Chandra et al. [41] reported 111.6% increase in methane
produced from alkali pretreated wheat straw (4% NaOH, 37 C for
120 h), which is much lower than the increase by the combined
pretreatments in the present work.
The impact of aerobic digestion pretreatment (Table 3) on
methane
production
was
the
highest
among
the
other
pretreatment methods applied. In fact, the biological pretreatment
can be considered as a preliminary digestion stage, in which hy-
drolysis and acidogenesis steps are performed at aerobic conditions
prior to the main anaerobic digestion stage. Hydrolysis and acido-
genesis stages are performed by facultative and obligatorily
anaerobic bacteria. The involved microorganisms in this pre-
liminary aerobic digestion stage (biological pretreatment) are the
facultative anaerobic bacteria, which have a higher growth rate
compared to the obligatorily anaerobic ones [42]. In other words,
this process can be considered as two-stage digestion that hydro-
lysis and acidogenesis phases were aerobically performed in the
ﬁrst stage, and acetogenesis and methanogenesis phases were
anaerobically performed in the second stage. This two-stage aero-
bic-anaerobic digestion process was expected to have higher re-
action rates compared to the conventional anaerobic digestion
processes, which was conﬁrmed by the results (Fig. 4). The inter-
mediate products of acidogenesis phase are VFAs. The high con-
centration of TVFAs after aerobic digestion conﬁrmed that the
hydrolysis and acidogenesis steps were the main bioreactions in
this pretreatment. To evaluate the efﬁciency of the proposed pre-
treatment in more details, techno-economic analysis and life cycle
assessment are suggetsed for the future work.
Ultrasonic pretreatment besides other pretreatments, especially
biological pretreatment, synergistically improved methane yield
from pinewood. However, its individual effect was not signiﬁcant.
This improvement is because of the physical breakdown of the
lignocellulose structure after the bubbles exploitation, which
consequently increases the conversion rate of complex organic
compounds into simple degradable compounds. Furthermore, the
implementation of these waves after aerobic digestion destroys the
aerobic sludge, decreases the particle size and, also intensiﬁes the
reduction of the volatile sludge solids. These changes cause a sig-
niﬁcant increase in sludge biodegradability during anaerobic
digestion and increasing biogas production [43,44]. Another
involved mechanism is the co-digestion of pinewood and aerobic
sludge, which can improve the methane yield by adjusting C/N
ratio. Pansripong et al. [45] showed that using ultrasonic waves at
frequencies of 37 and 102 kHz increased methane produced from
rice straw by 21.8% and 18.75%, respectively. This increase in
methane production was reported due to the removal of hemicel-
lulose during the ultrasonic pretreatment.
The efﬁciency of methane production depends on various fac-
tors such as type of pretreatment, pretreatment conditions,
anaerobic digestion temperature conditions, and substrate type.

study was unprecedented among the published papers on pine-

yields obtained in this research were within a low range. The
observed low range can be corresponded to the growth conditions
of the applied pinewood in this research. In other words, many
parameters affect the digestibility of lignocellulose from the same
species, such as the weather, soil quality, irrigation, and harvest
season.

5. Conclusions
The aerobic digestion applied as a pretreatment considerably
improved methane production yield from the softwood waste. The
combination of this biological pretreatment with mild chemical
and physical pretreatments synergistically increased biogas pro-
duction up to 1120%, from 4.6 mL/g VS for untreated pinewood to
50.4 mL/g VS. The biological pretreatment enhances the methane
yields by not only disrupting the biomass structure but the aerobic
sludge produced during the process also plays a role as a co-
substrate that can improve biogas yield by co-digestion mecha-
nism. The high concentration of total volatile fatty acids after aer-
obic digestion revealed that the biological pretreatment prior to
anaerobic digestion was, in fact, a two-stage digestion process, in
which hydrolysis and acidogenesis stages were performed in the
ﬁrst stage, and acetogenesis and methanogenesis stages were
performed in the second stage. Because of the higher rates of the
aerobic bioreactions than that of anaerobic conﬁguration, this
proposed two-stage aerobic-anaerobic digestion should have a
higher degradation rate compared to the conventional two-stage
anaerobic digestion. However, further research is needed to
conﬁrm this hypothesis.
